hints: Look carefully at the two humps on the graph. Which hump is lower, and what does an enzyme always do to that hump?
Remember activation energy is measured from the starting reactant energy level straight up to the top of the hump you are using.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two reaction pathways**

Think of this graph like two hills to climb. The tall hill is the reaction without an enzyme. The shorter hill is the reaction with an enzyme, because enzymes lower the barrier.

So the lower peak is the enzyme-catalysed pathway.

**Recall what activation energy means**

Activation energy is the extra energy reactants need to reach the top of the hill. It is always measured from the reactant baseline up to the peak.

$$activation\ energy = energy\ of\ peak - energy\ of\ reactants$$

**Match the labels to the enzyme pathway**

Label 2 goes exactly from the reactant level up to the lower (enzyme) peak. That is the new, smaller activation energy.

Label 1 is just how much the peak was lowered, and 1 + 2 together would be the old activation energy without enzyme.

options.A: 1 + 2 is the distance from reactants to the tall peak, so this is the activation energy without the enzyme, not with it.
options.B: 2 only goes from the reactant energy up to the lower enzyme peak, which is exactly the activation energy when enzyme is added.
options.C: 3 - 2 does not measure from reactants to a peak, it mixes a peak-to-product distance with activation energy, so it has no meaning here.
options.D: 4 goes from products all the way up to the tall non-enzyme peak, so it is not an activation energy at all.
